Can a squatter take ownership of a Vermont house?

Yes, in theory. Vermont recognizes adverse possession, so a person who occupies land in the right way for the full statutory period can ask a court to recognize title. The period is 15 years, and the claim is hard to win.

The 15-year number comes from the limitations statute for suing to recover land. 12 V.S.A. 501 says an action for the recovery of lands, or the possession of them, must be commenced within 15 years after the cause of action first accrues to the plaintiff, with an exception for cases covered by 32 V.S.A. 5263. If the true owner never sues inside that window, the occupier's position can ripen into title.

Most people who search for Vermont squatters rights are really asking one of three things. Someone is living in a house the owner does not control. A neighbor has been using part of a lot for decades. Or a former tenant will not leave. Vermont law treats these differently, and the right fix depends on which one you have.

What must a person prove to win adverse possession in Vermont?

The occupier carries the burden of proof on every element. In Mahoney v. Tara, LLC, 2014 VT 90, the Vermont Supreme Court said the claimant must show use or possession of the disputed land in an open, notorious, hostile and continuous manner for the full fifteen-year period.

The same opinion says the fifteen years is part of the claimant's own case, not a defense the title owner has to raise. It also describes adverse possession as a common-law claim for recognition of title, so a court is confirming something that already happened, not creating new rights.

ElementWhat it asksWhy it matters to an owner
OpenUse that anyone could seeRegular visits to the lot, even occasional, give you the chance to notice and object
NotoriousUse that is known in the communityNeighbors and town officials may be able to say who has been using the land
HostileUse without the owner's permissionA written permission or a lease can cut against this element
ContinuousUse through the full 15 yearsGaps in use can break the period

Source for the table: the court's statement of the standard in Mahoney v. Tara, LLC. The right-hand column is our plain-language reading, not the court's wording.

How does the 15-year clock work, and what stops it?

The clock stops when the title owner brings a claim, not when the occupier does. Mahoney held that only a title owner's claim against the possessor tolls the period. The possessor's own suit to quiet title does not.

In that case, the owner's motion to dismiss, which asserted ownership and gave the other side adequate notice, tolled the period in January 2008 before fifteen years had run. The trial court had added two separate stretches of possession that together came to less than thirteen years. The Supreme Court did not decide whether adding them together was proper, because it resolved the case on tolling.

For a seller, the practical lesson is simple. If you find a stranger on your land, write down the date you first learned of it, and act in writing. Silence for a decade or more is what gives these claims their force.

How does a Vermont owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

Vermont uses a court process called ejectment, and an owner who wins gets a writ of possession. Chapter 169 of Title 12 sets out the steps, and the Superior Court handles the case.

  • Under 12 V.S.A. 4854, a winning plaintiff receives judgment for possession, rents due, damages and costs. Attorney's fees may be added if a written rental agreement allows them.
  • The writ issues on the judgment date unless the court stays it for good cause.
  • The sheriff serves the writ and may not put the plaintiff in possession earlier than 14 days after service.
  • Under section 4854a, a landlord may dispose of belongings left behind without notice or liability 15 days after the writ is served or possession is restored, whichever is later.

Self-help is a poor idea. For tenants, 9 V.S.A. 4463 bars a landlord from cutting off utilities, locking the tenant out or withholding the tenant's belongings except through proper judicial process. The Vermont Judiciary states it directly: a landlord may not remove a tenant without a court order.

What if the occupant is a tenant or a subtenant?

A tenant who stays past the end of a lease is not a squatter in the adverse possession sense, because the stay began with the owner's permission. The owner uses the eviction route described by the Vermont Judiciary.

  • Give written notice that states the grounds and a termination date. Delivery can be by hand, first-class mail to the last known address, or certified mail.
  • Wait until the termination date passes, then file within 60 days or send a new notice.
  • File the complaint for ejectment in the Civil Division of the Superior Court in the county where the property sits, with the lease and the notice attached.
  • Arrange for a sheriff or constable to serve the papers. The tenant generally has 21 days after service to answer.
  • If the landlord wins, the sheriff serves the writ. The tenant generally has 14 days to leave, or 7 days if the case rests on a missed rent escrow payment.

Section 4853b adds a faster track for an unlawful occupant who has no right or permission to be in a unit where the lease bars subleasing. The hearing comes after 10 days' notice, and a writ lets the sheriff act not sooner than five days after service. The defendant can still oppose by showing a genuine dispute of fact.

The Judiciary's landlord and tenant page does not address squatters, so for a true stranger in the house it points people to the court's Access and Resource Center or VTLawHelp.

What are betterments, and why do they matter in an ejectment case?

Betterments are a counterclaim for the value of improvements an occupier made to land they honestly thought they owned. Under 12 V.S.A. 4811, the defendant in an ejectment action asserts it, and recovery depends on the owner winning the ejectment claim.

The value is measured by how much the improvements increased the land's value. The statute does not use the words good faith, but it requires that the defendant, or someone the defendant claims under, bought the land believing the title to be good or took a lease believing it conveyed the interest it described.

For a seller, that means a long-running dispute over a rebuilt garage, a new septic system or a barn can add a money claim on top of the title question. A buyer who inherits the problem inherits the claim too.

What does the Vermont housing picture look like for owners?

Vermont is a small, mostly owner-occupied state, which shapes how disputes about occupancy play out. Census figures show the scale.

MeasureVermont
Population estimate, July 1, 2025644,663
Households, 2020 to 2024273,416
Owner-occupied housing unit rate, 2020 to 202473.2%
Median value of owner-occupied units, 2020 to 2024$316,600

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts. The state covers about 9,600 square miles, entered the Union on March 4, 1791 as the 14th state, and relies on dairy, forestry, maple syrup and tourism. A house that sits unchecked for years is the usual setting for an occupancy dispute.

What should you do before selling a Vermont house with an occupant or boundary question?

Clear the occupancy or boundary issue first, or sell to a buyer who will take the house as it stands. Unresolved possession claims make a sale harder, and a deed has to meet Vermont's formal requirements to be recorded.

Under 27 V.S.A. 341, a deed must be signed by the grantor, acknowledged before a notary public and recorded in the land records of the town where the land lies. If the deed refers to a survey made or revised after July 1, 1988, the survey must accompany it or be cited by volume and page. Conveyances after January 1, 2020 that subdivide a parcel or change its boundaries need a plat or a citation to one.

Taxes come next. The Vermont Department of Taxes administers the property transfer tax, and payment is due within 30 days of closing. The general rate is 1.25% plus a 0.22% clean water surcharge. A principal residence pays 0.5% on the first $200,000 and 1.47% above that. A non-principal home fit for year-round use that is not a long-term rental pays 3.40%, or 3.62% with the surcharge. The rate depends on how the property is used, so confirm it with the Department before closing.

If you own a Vermont house with a squatter, a tenant who will not leave or an inherited property no one has visited, a cash buyer can purchase as-is. We do not give legal advice, and an attorney should review any title question before you sign.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter claim my Vermont house after a few years?

No. Vermont uses a 15-year period under 12 V.S.A. 501, and the occupier must prove open, notorious, hostile and continuous use for all of it. A few years of occupancy does not meet that standard.

Do I need a court order to remove someone from my Vermont property?

Yes, if the person is a tenant, and in practice for any occupant who refuses to leave. Vermont law bars landlords from lockouts and utility shutoffs outside proper judicial process, and a writ of possession is served by the sheriff.

How long after a Vermont eviction judgment does the occupant have to leave?

Generally 14 days after the sheriff serves the writ of possession under 12 V.S.A. 4854. A missed rent escrow payment shortens that to 7 days, and the unlawful occupant track in section 4853b uses five days.

Does giving permission stop an adverse possession claim?

Permission cuts against the hostile element, because the use is no longer against the owner's rights. Written permission, a lease or a signed license is easier to prove later than a verbal okay.

Who pays Vermont property transfer tax when I sell?

Payment is due within 30 days of the closing date, and the rate depends on how the property is used.

What happens to tenants when a Vermont landlord sells a rental?

A sale does not by itself end a tenancy in Vermont, and the landlord still needs a legal reason and a written notice to end it. The state's residential rental law sits in Title 9, Chapter 137, and the rules below come from the statutes and the Vermont Judiciary.

The one provision that speaks to a sale directly is 9 V.S.A. § 4467(d). A landlord who has contracted to sell the building may end a tenancy that has no written rental agreement on at least 30 days of actual notice.

Security deposits move with the property. When the landlord's interest ends, the deposit must be transferred to the new landlord, who must give the tenant actual notice of the new landlord's name and address (9 V.S.A. § 4461(f)).

How much notice does a Vermont landlord have to give?

The notice period depends on the reason and on whether there is a written lease. Section 4467 sets these periods.

SituationNotice
Nonpayment of rent14 days
Breach of a material lease term30 days before the termination date
Criminal, drug or violent activity that threatens other residents14 days
No written agreement, monthly rent, tenant of two years or less60 days
No written agreement, monthly rent, tenant of more than two years90 days
No written agreement, weekly rent21 days
No written agreement, landlord has contracted to sell the building30 days
Written lease, no-cause ending, tenant of two years or less30 days before the end of the stated term
Written lease, no-cause ending, tenant of more than two years60 days before the end of the stated term

The notice must state the termination date. An eviction case must be filed within 60 days of the termination date in the notice, or the notice cannot support a judgment. Accepting rent after termination generally does not waive the landlord's remedies for breach or no-cause termination, and accepting partial rent does not waive remedies for nonpayment.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities to speed up a sale?

No. The Vermont Judiciary states that a landlord may not remove a tenant without a court order, and may not change the locks, shut off utilities or remove belongings without one, citing 9 V.S.A. § 4463.

A written notice can be delivered by hand, by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address, or by certified mail. Some towns require more notice than the statute, and subsidized rentals such as Section 8 carry extra requirements, so check the lease and any program rules.

What does the Vermont eviction process look like?

An eviction, which Vermont calls ejectment, is filed in the Civil Division of the Superior Court in the county where the property sits. The Judiciary's page describes these steps.

  1. Serve a written termination notice with the grounds and the termination date.
  2. Wait until the date passes, then file within 60 days with the complaint, a copy of the lease if written, the notice, and the CARES Act declaration (form 100-00031).
  3. A sheriff or constable serves the tenant, and the landlord files the return of service.
  4. The tenant generally has 21 days after service to file a written answer. If none is filed, the landlord may seek a default judgment.
  5. A judge decides at hearing or trial whether the tenant can be evicted and whether either side owes money.
  6. If the landlord wins, the court issues a writ of possession, and the tenant has 14 days after service to leave.

A landlord can ask the court to order past-due rent paid into escrow while the case is pending (12 V.S.A. § 4853a). If the tenant misses a payment, the landlord is entitled to immediate possession and the tenant must leave within 7 days. A writ is effective for 60 days after it issues, and the landlord may dispose of remaining belongings on the later of 15 days after the writ is served or the date the landlord legally retakes possession.

The timeline matters to a seller because a buyer who wants vacant possession may wait for a case to run its course. Either side may appeal legal errors to the Vermont Supreme Court.

What are a tenant's rights while the landlord is trying to sell?

A tenant keeps the same protections whether or not the house is listed. They include the implied warranty of habitability, protection from retaliation, and rules on rent increases and deposits.

  • Under 9 V.S.A. § 4457, the landlord is treated as promising premises that are safe, clean and fit for human habitation, and a rental agreement cannot waive this promise. The unit needs heat that can safely provide a reasonable amount of warmth, and adequate water with hot and cold lines.
  • Under § 4465, a landlord may not retaliate against a tenant who complains to a government agency about a health or safety violation, complains to the landlord about a violation, or joins a tenant group. A termination notice within 90 days of a municipal or state violation notice, for reasons other than unpaid rent, is presumed retaliatory.
  • Under § 4455, rent is due without demand, and a rent increase takes effect on the first day of the next rental period after at least 60 days of actual notice.
  • Under § 4456, a tenant must not damage the premises or interfere with other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, and can end a tenancy by giving actual notice at least one rental payment period before the termination date unless the lease says otherwise.

A landlord who files a notice to sell soon after a code complaint should expect the retaliation presumption to come up.

What are the Vermont security deposit rules?

A landlord must return the deposit with a written itemized statement within 14 days after learning the tenant has moved out or abandoned the unit, or after the move-out date if the tenant gave notice. Seasonal rentals that are not a primary residence get 60 days.

A landlord may keep money only for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear and tear, unpaid utility or other charges owed, and removal of abandoned articles. If the landlord misses the 14 days, the right to withhold any part is lost, and a willful failure makes the landlord liable for double the amount wrongfully withheld plus attorney's fees and costs. A tenant who is owed a deposit can use small claims court for up to $10,000, and Brattleboro and Burlington have additional deposit rules.

For a seller, an accurate deposit ledger is part of the closing package, because the buyer takes over the duty to return each deposit.

Who inspects Vermont rentals, and what does that mean before a sale?

The Division of Fire Safety, within the Department of Public Safety, is the primary enforcer of the Rental Housing Health and Safety Code under Act 181, signed June 7, 2022, and the program took effect January 1, 2024. Local health officials keep concurrent authority and can still inspect.

The program is complaint-based. Tenants first contact the owner or manager, and if that fails they can submit an online complaint form that routes to the regional office for the property's ZIP code. The Division has regional offices in Williston, Waterbury, Rutland and Springfield. Short-term rentals count as rentals, but the Division inspects them only in response to complaints.

What tax and reporting items does a landlord face when selling a Vermont rental?

Landlords who rent residential property for 30 or more days in a row file a Landlord Certificate (Form LRC-140) with the Department of Taxes each year for each property with a rented unit. A landlord who does not file may be fined, with interest.

On the sale itself, the Department of Taxes lists the property transfer tax at 1.25 percent for a year-round home that is a long-term rental, and 3.40 percent for a non-principal residence fit for year-round habitation that is not a long-term rental. Add the 0.22 percent Clean Water Surcharge in both cases, and ask your attorney which category your building falls into. Vermont also treats a landlord's certificate carefully: under 32 V.S.A. § 9602 the Commissioner may assess the higher rate if a landlord certificate is filed without a real landlord-tenant relationship.

A nonresident landlord should expect 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price, filed by the buyer on Form RW-171 within 30 days, unless a Commissioner's Certificate is obtained.

Where can landlords and tenants get help in Vermont?

The Judiciary lists three starting points: the Access and Resource Center at 802-879-1185 or selfhelp@vtcourts.gov, the CVOEO tenant hotline at 802-864-0099, and Vermont Legal Aid at 800-889-2047.

Vermont has 14 counties, and a case is filed in the county where the rental sits. Chittenden County, which includes Burlington, had 168,323 residents in the 2020 Census and is the most populous. Median gross rent statewide was $1,234 for 2020 to 2024, and the median value of owner-occupied homes was $316,600, according to the Census Bureau.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Vermont landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?

Only with proper notice. If there is no written agreement and the landlord has contracted to sell the building, 9 V.S.A. § 4467(d) allows at least 30 days of actual notice.

How many days does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Vermont?

14 days after learning the tenant moved out, or after the move-out date if notice was given, with an itemized written statement. Seasonal rentals get 60 days.

How much notice is needed for nonpayment of rent?

14 days under 9 V.S.A. § 4467(a). A written lease does not lengthen it.

Does the deposit transfer to the buyer?

Yes. Under § 4461(f), the deposit transfers to the new landlord, who must give the tenant actual notice of the name and address.

Can a Vermont landlord remove a tenant without going to court?

No. The Judiciary says a landlord may not remove a tenant, change locks, shut off utilities or remove belongings without a court order.

How long does a tenant have to leave after a writ of possession?

14 days after service of the writ, or 7 days after a missed rent escrow payment.
